summary: An April 1 humorous document explaining the origins of the words foo, bar, and foobar, which appear as placeholder names in about 212 RFCs. It is informational.

eli5.summary: People use silly words like foo as stand-in names. This funny note explains where those words came from.

subtitle: An April 1st exploration of the mysterious origins of metasyntactic variables foo, bar, and foobar.

tldr.problem: Approximately 212 RFCs use the terms foo, bar, and foobar as placeholder names without explanation, confusing newcomers to the Internet standards community.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3092 traces these words through comics, cartoons, World War II military slang, and hacker culture. Foo probably comes from the 1930s Smokey Stover comic by Bill Holman, while foobar may have been influenced by the military acronym FUBAR (Fucked Up Beyond All Recognition).
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the playful naming convention used throughout technical writing, showing how a 1930s nonsense word from popular culture became embedded in computer culture through multiple independent traditions.

today: RFC 3092 is an April 1st informational RFC published 1 April 2001, presented with scholarly detail but entirely for humor. The metasyntactic variables foo, bar, and related words remain in use throughout computing.

sections.title: The Mystery of Foo and Bar
sections.content:
RFC 3092 is an April 1st joke RFC that rectifies a quirk of the RFC series: approximately 7% of RFCs, or about 212 RFCs at the time of writing, contain the metasyntactic variables foo, bar, or foobar without explanation. The RFC traces the origins of these words with scholarly rigor, despite their humorous nature.

The word foo appears to have multiple independent sources: a 1930s comic strip, World War II military graffiti, and early computer hacker culture. Bar is the second metasyntactic variable, and foobar likely combines both words.
sections.eli5: People use silly words as placeholder names in computer instructions. This document seriously traces where these words came from, starting from old cartoons.

sections.title: Comic Strips to World War II
sections.content:
The earliest documented uses of foo were in the surrealist Smokey Stover comic strip by Bill Holman about a fireman, published between about 1930 and 1952. The comic featured nonsense phrases including FOO on license plates and in background graffiti, with catchphrases like "He who foos last foos best" and Smokey saying "Where there's foo, there's fire." Holman reportedly claimed to have found the word on the bottom of a Chinese figurine.

During World War II, foo appeared in both British and US military slang. British troops used the graffito "FOO was here" similar to the American "Kilroy." In 1944-45, radar operators used the term foo fighters for mysterious radar traces, later called UFOs. The RFC notes that foobar was probably influenced by the military acronym FUBAR, though the word foo itself predates this.
sections.eli5: A cartoonist in the 1930s filled his comics with the nonsense word foo. During World War II, soldiers used it as graffiti and to describe mysterious radar signals.

sections.title: Entry into Computer Culture
sections.content:
By 1959, the word foo was documented in the TMRC (Tech Model Railroad Club at MIT) dictionary as "the sacred syllable" and an in-joke with Tibetan Buddhism undertones. Early computer engineers at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) popularized foobar as a metasyntactic variable in system manuals during the 1960s and 1970s. The RFC notes that foobar may have spread partly because it parses in electronics jargon as an inverted foo signal.

The RFC lists other metasyntactic variables in standard use: baz, qux, quux, corge, grault, garply, waldo, fred, plugh, xyzzy, and thud.
sections.eli5: MIT students used foo as an inside joke in the 1950s. Computer companies then put foobar in their instruction books, and it stuck in programming culture forever.
